questions.prompt: A production autonomous vehicle perception model reliably detects obstacles under clear daytime conditions, but fails to identify a pedestrian at dusk even though all code executes without exceptions and strictly within its 50 ms latency window. Which core challenge does this failure demonstrate?

options.label: Latency added by serial interconnect communication across accelerators
A hardware execution failure caused by GPU thermal throttling
The dual mandate: learned behaviour must stay statistically trustworthy while executing within physical budgets
The failure of CI pipelines to compile SGD operations

questions.explanation: Everything executed correctly; the learned behaviour itself was untrustworthy under shifted conditions. The dual mandate requires *both* statistical trustworthiness and physical delivery. (a) and (b) are machine faults that monitoring would catch; (d) is a category error.

questions.prompt: Which historical transition correctly pairs an AI era with the systems bottleneck that limited its scale?
questions.explanation: Statistical ML (SVMs over SIFT/HOG features) was limited by hand-engineered features. Symbolic AI hit the *logic* bottleneck, expert systems the *knowledge-acquisition* bottleneck, deep learning the *infrastructure* bottleneck; the options swap the first two on purpose.

questions.prompt: Google Flu Trends had access to hundreds of billions of real-time search queries and still failed. Why, and what does the failure say about data volume as a substitute for ground truth?
questions.modelAnswer: The proxy drifted: query volume measured public attention and product behaviour (autocomplete, news coverage), not influenza incidence: 2× the CDC rate in 2012–13, overestimating 100 of 108 weeks from Aug 2011. Data volume is not ground truth: a behavioural proxy needs a feedback loop to a trusted measurement and continual re-validation.

questions.prompt: In the degradation equation $\mathrm{Acc}(t) \approx \mathrm{Acc}_0 - \lambda\, D(P_t \,\|\, P_0)$, what does the term $\lambda$ represent?

options.label: The learning rate used during model training
The sensitivity of accuracy to distribution divergence, fitted locally
The fraction of the dataset reserved for validation
The decay constant of the hardware's thermal envelope

questions.explanation: λ is a locally-fitted sensitivity: how much accuracy drops per unit of observed divergence. It is estimated from observed shifts/outcomes, not a universal constant, which is also why the equation is a local trend, not a law.

questions.prompt: When data transfers and arithmetic overlap in a pipelined runtime, which expression gives the lower bound on execution time?
questions.explanation: Ideal overlap hides the faster stage behind the slower: the bound is max of the two plus non-overlapped overhead. (a) is the sequential model.

questions.prompt: Improving initial training accuracy $\mathrm{Acc}_0$, with drift sensitivity $\lambda$ held fixed, is sufficient to guarantee the model resists production distribution shift. True or false, and say why.

options.label: True: a higher floor means slower effective decay

questions.explanation: A better baseline doesn't establish robustness to drift: $\mathrm{Acc}_0$ and $\lambda$ are separate quantities in the equation. Better data/objectives can lower $\lambda$, but only evaluating under the shifted conditions establishes it. (Holding $\lambda$ fixed, a higher $\mathrm{Acc}_0$ just decays from a higher floor.)

questions.prompt: Explain the iron law of ML systems to a junior engineer who knows Python but has never profiled hardware. Use the three factors by name.
questions.modelAnswer: Every ML task takes wall-clock time equal to three multiplied factors: $T = \frac{\text{samples}}{\text{task}} \times \frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{sample}} \times \frac{s}{\text{FLOP}}$: how many samples the task processes (Data), how much arithmetic each sample needs (Algorithm), and how fast the machine really executes each operation (Machine). The last factor isn't the datasheet peak: it unpacks into bytes moved over bandwidth, operations over realised rate, plus fixed overhead: $T \approx D_{\mathrm{vol}}/BW + O/(R_{\mathrm{peak}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{hw}}) + L_{\mathrm{lat}}$. So "make it faster" means: fewer samples, fewer FLOPs per sample, or a higher realised rate, and the right lever is whichever term currently dominates.

questions.prompt: "The model is not the system." Explain what that means using the spam filter that has to keep working while spammers change tactics.
questions.modelAnswer: The classifier's learned weights are maybe a few percent of the production system. Around them sit ingestion, labelling, feature pipelines, training, deployment, serving, and monitoring, each carrying assumptions no model test exercises. When a new phishing template appears, the data layer must capture it, training must absorb it, and serving must ship the update inside the latency budget. Any of those can fail while the model code is untouched; the failures live at the interfaces.

questions.prompt: Why is a benchmark score statistical evidence rather than proof of production readiness? Bring in the verification gap.
questions.modelAnswer: A test set is a sample of the input space, and the space is unenumerable: ImageNet's 50,000 validation images against 256^150,528 possible inputs. A score is statistical evidence about the population the sample represents, and production populations drift. So a score supports a deployment claim only for the stated population and protocol, and needs monitoring to keep holding.

questions.prompt:
A sequential job on one accelerator moves 20 GB at 800 GB/s, performs 40 GFLOP at an effective rate of 400 GFLOP/s, and pays 5 ms of fixed overhead.

a) What is the predicted sequential execution time $T_{\mathrm{seq}} = T_{\mathrm{mem}} + T_{\mathrm{comp}} + T_{\mathrm{ovh}}$? Which term dominates?

b) With ideal overlap of movement and compute (overhead stays outside), what is the lower bound $T_{\mathrm{ovl}} = \max(T_{\mathrm{mem}}, T_{\mathrm{comp}}) + T_{\mathrm{ovh}}$?

c) You double bandwidth to 1600 GB/s. Recompute both numbers. What did the upgrade actually buy, and what binds now?

d) The vendor offers a 2× arithmetic rate instead of the bandwidth upgrade. Same total spend. Which do you pick and why?
questions.modelAnswer:
a) Movement = 20 GB / 800 GB/s = 25 ms; compute = 40 / 400 = 100 ms; overhead 5 ms, so **T ≈ 130 ms, compute-dominated.**

b) `max(25, 100) + 5` = **105 ms**.

c) Movement = 12.5 ms, sequential = 117.5 ms; overlap bound = 105 ms (compute still binds). The bandwidth upgrade bought ~12.5 ms sequential and **nothing** on the ideal bound; arithmetic now sets the ceiling.

d) Take the 2× arithmetic: compute drops to 50 ms, sequential 80 ms, overlap bound 55 ms. Compute was the dominant term; improving the smaller term (memory) is the classic Amdahl mistake, since you only ever gain through the share of time the upgraded part occupies.
